lead: Internal energy U is the energy stored inside matter: the kinetic energy of its molecules plus the potential energy of the forces between them. Enthalpy H = U + pV adds the flow work pV to U. The two terms always appear together when mass crosses a boundary, so H gets its own name. You meet u in a rigid tank and h in boilers, turbines and heat exchangers. Both are state properties, in kJ or, per kilogram, in kJ/kg.
prereq: You need: the first law for a closed system, Q − W = ΔU, and the ideal-gas equation pV = mRT.

sections.h3: Internal energy is energy stored inside matter

blocks.text: Internal energy U is the sum of the kinetic energy of the molecules (translation, rotation, vibration) and the potential energy of the forces between them. It does not include the kinetic or potential energy of the whole system moving or raised. The unit is kJ, and the specific internal energy is u = U/m in kJ/kg, where m is the mass in kg.

U is a state property. For a simple substance two independent properties fix the state, and so fix u: pressure and temperature in a single-phase gas or liquid, but pressure and dryness fraction in a wet steam mixture, where p and T are tied together. U is extensive: doubling the mass doubles U. Thermodynamics never needs absolute U, only changes ΔU.
For an ideal gas the molecules exert no forces on one another, so u depends on temperature alone and

blocks.where: m is the mass (kg); c<sub>v</sub> is the specific heat at constant volume (kJ/kg·K); ΔT is the final minus the initial temperature (K); ΔU is in kJ. Valid for an ideal gas with constant c<sub>v</sub>.

blocks.text: For steam and refrigerants u also depends on pressure, so it is read from property tables (see Steam tables and Mollier chart).

sections.h3: Enthalpy adds flow work to internal energy

blocks.text: Fluid entering a control volume is pushed in by the fluid behind it. That push-in work per kg is pv, where p is the absolute pressure in kPa and v the specific volume in m³/kg (kPa × m³/kg = kJ/kg). Each entering kilogram carries its internal energy u and this flow work pv. Enthalpy bundles them:
H = U + pV,  h = u + pv
blocks.where: H is the enthalpy (kJ), U the internal energy (kJ), p the absolute pressure (kPa), V the volume (m³); h, u and v are the same per kilogram (kJ/kg, kJ/kg, m³/kg).

blocks.text: Take changes: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV). For an ideal gas pV = mRT, where R is the gas constant in kJ/kg·K, so Δ(pV) = mRΔT and ΔH = m(cv + R)ΔT = mcpΔT. Why cp − cv = R is shown in Specific heats of gases.

Three places where heat equals an enthalpy change: a closed system at constant pressure with only boundary work (Q = ΔH); a steady-flow heater, boiler or condenser with no shaft work and negligible changes of kinetic and potential energy (q = h₂ − h₁); and a phase change at constant pressure, where the latent heat is an enthalpy change such as h<sub>fg</sub> for steam.
Enthalpy is not heat. “Heat content” is a loose old name. Heat Q is energy in transit and depends on the path; H is a state property. Q equals ΔH only in the cases above.
Read the process before choosing a formula.

examples.question: 2 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. Find ΔU, ΔH and Δ(pV), and the heat supplied.
steps: Data: m = 2 kg, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K, so ΔT = 100 K.
Δ(pV) = mRΔT = 2 × 0.287 × 100 = 57.4 kJ. At constant pressure this is also the boundary work W = pΔV.
Constant pressure, closed system: Q = ΔH = 201.0 kJ. The first law agrees: Q = ΔU + W = 143.6 + 57.4 = 201.0 kJ.
examples.answer: ΔU = 143.6 kJ, ΔH = 201.0 kJ, Δ(pV) = 57.4 kJ, and the heat supplied is 201.0 kJ.

examples.question: Steam tables give, for dry saturated steam at 1 MPa (1000 kPa): u<sub>g</sub> = 2582.8 kJ/kg and v<sub>g</sub> = 0.1944 m³/kg. Find h<sub>g</sub> from h = u + pv.
steps: Flow work: pv = 1000 kPa × 0.1944 m³/kg = 194.4 kJ/kg.
The table lists h<sub>g</sub> = 2777.1 kJ/kg at 1 MPa; the 0.1 kJ/kg gap is rounding of v.
examples.answer: h<sub>g</sub> = 2777.2 kJ/kg, which matches the table: about 7 % of the enthalpy of this steam is flow work.

traps: Using ΔH = mc<sub>p</sub>ΔT as the heat for a closed rigid tank. A rigid tank has Q = ΔU = mc<sub>v</sub>ΔT.
Adding R = 287 J/kg·K to c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K. Convert R to 0.287 kJ/kg·K first.
Writing ΔH = ΔU + pΔV in every process. The general form is ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV); pΔV is enough only at constant pressure.
Writing q = Δh for a nozzle because it has no shaft work. There q = 0 and the enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy.
Using c<sub>p</sub>ΔT for steam or refrigerants. Their h depends on both T and p; read it from tables.

quiz.q: Define internal energy U and give its unit.
quiz.a: U is the energy stored inside matter: molecular kinetic energy plus the potential energy of intermolecular forces, excluding the motion and height of the system as a whole. Unit kJ; specific internal energy u is in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Write the defining equations for H and h.
quiz.a: H = U + pV and h = u + pv, with p the absolute pressure, V the volume and v the specific volume; H in kJ, h in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Why does enthalpy bundle the pV term with internal energy?
quiz.a: Fluid entering a control volume carries its u plus the push-in flow work pv done by the fluid behind it. The two always travel together when mass crosses a boundary, so h = u + pv is the useful single property.

quiz.q: Why is “heat content” a poor name for enthalpy?
quiz.a: Heat is energy in transit and depends on the path; enthalpy is a state property. Q = ΔH only for special cases such as a constant-pressure closed process with only boundary work.

quiz.q: 1.5 kg of air (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is heated at constant pressure through 80 K. Find ΔU, ΔH and Δ(pV).
0.5 kg of air in a rigid tank (c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is heated through 50 K. Find Q and ΔH.
quiz.a: Rigid tank: W = 0, so Q = ΔU = 0.5 × 0.718 × 50 = 17.95 kJ. ΔH = 0.5 × 1.005 × 50 = 25.13 kJ. Q is not ΔH here; the extra 7.18 kJ is Δ(pV) = V Δp, not heat.

quiz.q: A student uses Δh = c<sub>p</sub>ΔT for steam in a boiler. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Steam near saturation is not an ideal gas; its h depends on both pressure and temperature, and the water changes phase in the boiler, where T stays constant while h rises by h<sub>fg</sub>. Use steam tables: Δh = h₂ − h₁.

quiz.q: For an ideal gas, why do u and h depend only on temperature?
quiz.a: With no intermolecular forces there is no potential energy between molecules, so u is molecular kinetic energy, set by T alone. Since pv = RT, h = u + RT is also a function of T alone.

beyond: Enthalpy is the working property of boilers, condensers, evaporators and heat exchangers; steam tables and the Mollier chart list h directly. Chemical engineers use the standard enthalpy of formation for reactor energy balances, and air-conditioning engineers use the enthalpy of moist air in psychrometry. Search next for “enthalpy of steam”, “enthalpy of formation” and “moist air enthalpy”.
